speakers.name: Achille Roussel
speakers.bio:
Achille has worked as a software engineer on distributed systems since 2011, at both startups and large companies like Twitch, Facebook, Segment, and Twilio.

He has authored and participate in multiple open-source projects such as kafka-go, parquet-go, wazero, and also contributed the GOOS=wasip1 port of Go.

In 2024, Achille co-founded Firetiger to develop agents that help engineers manage their deployments, catalog issues, and apply remediations when defects make it to production.

speakers.name: Akshay Shah
speakers.bio: At Antithesis, Akshay helps companies build strong verification gates into software factories. Prior to Antithesis, he’s worked on infrastructure and developer experience at a variety of companies - including leading Uber’s Go team.

speakers.name: Alexander Baygeldin
speakers.bio: Alexander is a backend engineer at Evil Martians, where he helps startups build modern, scalable, and lasting web applications. Alexander has a passion for crafting clean and maintainable architectures.

speakers.name: Andrew Williams
speakers.bio:
Andrew Williams has over 20 years of commercial software development experience across a variety of programming languages and has been a core developer in large open source projects such as Enlightenment, EFL, Maven and Fyne. He has been a founding member of many startups including Scotland’s largest mobile apps agency. Since 2018 he has been focused on Go development and is working hard to apply the high quality design principles of mobile app development to cross-platform applications.

Andrew is the author of "Building Cross-Platform GUI Applications with Fyne" and "Hands-On GUI Application Development in Go" and is also the founder of the Fyne toolkit demonstrated in this presentation.

speakers.name: Austin Clements
speakers.bio:
As the technical lead for the Go programming language, Austin is responsible for the overall technical direction and governance of the Go project. Austin’s tenure at Google spans over a decade, with much of that time dedicated to deep-system contributions, including previously serving as the lead for the Go compiler and runtime. They have a long history with Go, including writing a Go interpreter and debugger as an intern in 2009 and developing Go’s concurrent garbage collector with Rick Hudson in 2015. Their recent focus includes optimizing Go for the latest hardware through projects like the Green Tea garbage collector and native SIMD support, establishing governance structures that serve both Go and the community better, and ensuring Go thrives in a world driven by both human and agentic programming. 

An MIT alumnus with a passion for how programming languages shape thought, Austin balances their work on Go with personal interests in smart home technology, mid-century modern architecture, and the decade-long pursuit of the perfect matcha latte.

speakers.name: Benji Vesterby
speakers.bio:
Benji fell in love with computers when he started early—building PCs, teaching himself to code, and chasing distributed systems, AI, and security. In 2017, he discovered Go at a SANS (SysAdmin, Audit, Network, and Security) conference and attended his first GopherCon a year later. The community’s pragmatism shaped Benji’s approach of shipping real code, measuring outcomes, and sharing what works. Today, he is the founder of and one of the masterminds behind the GopherCon Challenge Series and trains 160+ engineers a year.

Outside of work Benji is a photographer, PADI‑certified SCUBA diver and a relentless bread‑baker chasing the perfect sourdough.

speakers.name: Cameron Balahan
speakers.bio:
Cameron is the product lead for the Go programming language at Google and a contributor to Google’s agent ecosystem and AI developer assistance strategy. Before Go, he led Google Cloud's programming languages support and integrations. Before joining Google, Cameron led a high-frequency market-making firm where he built low-latency trading systems in C and C++. 

He likes Go more.

speakers.name: Casey Manus
speakers.bio:
Casey Manus is a Principal Engineer at Bayer Crop Science and a 30-year veteran of the software engineering industry. Having navigated three decades of evolving technology, Casey has seen countless trends come and go, giving him a unique perspective on building resilient systems that stand the test of time. Today, he applies that deep expertise to solving global agricultural challenges using Go.

A returning GopherCon speaker, Casey previously presented "Genetic Algorithms in Go" in 2023 and continues to remain heavily involved in the Go community and conference.  

Before his long career in tech, Casey served in the U.S. Navy aboard a nuclear fast-attack submarine, an experience that instilled a disciplined approach to complex engineering. Based in Miami, Casey spends his downtime embracing the Florida lifestyle, whether hanging out on his boat in the Florida Keys or enjoying the open water.

speakers.name: Cassie Coyle
speakers.bio:
Cassie Coyle is a Senior Software Engineer at Diagrid, where she works on the Dapr open source project, a graduated CNCF project, building the distributed systems foundation that keeps AI agents and workflows running in production. Cassie is a maintainer of the Dapr runtime and various core Dapr repositories and SDKs, helping shape the roadmap and architecture of the platform that powers durable workflows, crash-safe agents, and fault-tolerant microservices.

Cassie has built extensively across Dapr, including the distributed Scheduler - a horizontally scalable system for reliable job execution - and Workflow History Propagation, a first-of-its-kind capability that brings verifiable execution lineage and chain of custody to durable workflows. As a core member of the Dapr release team, she regularly cuts releases and drives cross-cutting initiatives spanning observability, SDKs, control plane services, and developer experience.

Before joining Diagrid, Cassie helped develop HashiCorp's Waypoint, streamlining application building, deployment, and release across platforms. Prior to that, she helped build out Charles Schwab's cloud infrastructure as part of a major initiative to migrate the company's applications,
including Schwab Bank, to the cloud, building and prototyping the infrastructure pipelines and automation that enabled the transition at scale.

In 2025, Cassie received the Society of Women Engineers (SWE) Rising Technical Contributor Award, given to only 20 women globally each year. Cassie serves on the Call for Papers review team for various conferences, is a member of Dapr Day 2023/2024 and AppDeveloperCon North America 2024 program committees, organizes the Women Who Go meetup in Austin, TX, and is a member of several Working Groups in the Linux Foundation Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). She enjoys mentoring contributors, and advocating for welcoming spaces for diverse contributors in open source.

She has spoken at major conferences including:

● 2024 GopherCon US: Standardizing Errors in Go: A Practical Guide with Dapr
● 2024 KubeCon NA: Scale Job Triggering with a Distributed Scheduler
● 2024 Open Source Summit: Standardizing Errors: A Practical Guide with Dapr
● 2024 Grace Hopper Celebration: Level Up Lab (Workshop): Spike Your Application Development Skills with Dapr
● 2022 Hashitalks Deploy: Use Waypoint to Easily Deploy to All Three Cloud Providers

Away from the keyboard, Cassie is a beekeeper tending a growing apiary of 7 hives, where she applies distributed systems patterns to build AI-assisted beekeeping tooling. She is part of a family of "gophers" and frequently attends technical conferences with her twin sister, Sam.

speakers.name: Chris Tarazi
speakers.bio: Chris is a senior staff software engineer at Isovalent@Cisco, where he has been a core contributor to the Cilium and eBPF project for over six years, focusing on networking and security.

speakers.name: Cory LaNou
speakers.bio:
Cory is a full stack technologist with nearly 30 years of professional experience. He began his career at CDW.com in the late 90's, where he helped build one of the world's first ecommerce engines, predating Amazon. He has started several technology companies, including Pulsity, a web consulting firm in the late 90's. From that company, Local Launch, an internet marketing technology company, was formed and later sold to RH Donnelly in 2006. 

Cory has years of experience in the Go world, having worked on the Core engineering team that contributes to InfluxDB, a highly scalable, distributed time series database written in Go. He has worked on several other Go projects with a focus on profiling and optimizing applications, using advanced profiling concepts such as torch graphs and tracing profiles. He also has deep ties to the Go community, having started one of the very first Go meetups in the world, Denver Gophers, as well as assisting in the very first GopherCon. He has created and led numerous Go workshops and training courses, has published several online articles related to Go, and co-authored "Go Fundamentals". Cory is also a partner at Gopher Guides, the industry leader for Go training and conferences.

When Cory isn't working on writing new Go training material, he volunteers as a high school AI Programming Club leader. He also volunteers his time helping local entrepreneurs start up their own businesses by offering free business advice and services, such as incorporating their business, getting their web presence set up, and giving them the moral support they need to make their dreams a reality.

speakers.name: Derek Parker
speakers.bio: Derek is the creator of Delve, the debugger for the Go programming language, and a contributor to the Go compiler and runtime. He has been developing software for over a decade and has traveled the world speaking at conferences and teaching workshops about debugging.

speakers.name: Derick Schaefer
speakers.bio:
Derick Schaefer is a technology leader, consultant, speaker, and author with more than 35 years of experience building enterprise software and leading engineering organizations. Introduced to Go in 2016, he has championed its adoption across SaaS companies for its simplicity, performance, and maintainability.

He is the author of CLI – A Practical Guide to Modern Command-Line Interfaces (https://moderncli.dev) and Integrating SaaS Acquisitions: A Technical Leader’s M&A Playbook. He is also an active open-source contributor, with projects including the RESERVE macroeconomics CLI, the PortableText package for Go, and Static Cache Wrangler for WordPress. Derick enjoys sharing practical lessons on Go, developer tooling, software design, and engineering leadership.

speakers.name: Donia Chaiehloudj
speakers.bio:
Donia Chaiehloudj is a Senior Software Engineer at Isovalent, where she contributes to the Cilium project, focusing on network policy and cloud-native networking. Her work sits at the intersection of Kubernetes, Linux networking, and eBPF, helping improve how distributed systems are secured and observed at scale. 

She is co-author of Learn Go with Pocket-Sized Projects and has a strong interest in sharing content around Go, networking and eBPF. Donia is also an active member of the developer community, leading a local meetup, organising conferences, serving as a Women Techmakers ambassador and part of the Merge-Forward, a diversity CNCF initiative. Outside of engineering, she enjoys sewing, playing the clarinet, and exploring new hiking trails.

speakers.name: Dylan Bourque
speakers.bio: Dylan has been a professional software developer since 1998, working in the banking, health care, finance, computer security, developer tooling, and now AI industries.  He’s been writing Go full time since early 2016. He is a part-time co-host of the Fallthrough podcast and is an active participant in the Gophers Slack organization. This will be his ninth GopherCon and his fifth time on stage.  Outside of work, Dylan enjoys baseball and golf.

speakers.name: Erik St. Martin
speakers.bio: Erik St. Martin spent the last decade building distributed systems for large enterprises such as cable providers, credit bureaus, and fraud detection companies, and now works for Microsoft as a Principal Software Engineer. He co-authored a book on the Go programming language, is the president of Gopher Academy, and emcees GopherCon, the annual conference for the Go community.

speakers.name: Filippo Valsorda
speakers.bio: Filippo is a cryptography engineer and open source maintainer. He’s been a maintainer of the Go cryptography standard library since 2018, first at Google as lead of the Go Security team, and now as the founder of Geomys, an organization of professional Go open source maintainers.

speakers.name: Florin Pățan
speakers.bio:
Florin is a consultant at Ardan Labs with over 12 years of Go experience. He's worked across distributed systems, application architecture, observability, and cloud infrastructure with time spent at fintech, healthcare, and AI companies like Bread Financial, Press Ganey, drand, and Prediction Guard.

He has worked at AI startups and enterprise companies where he built the infrastructure from the ground up and designed the systems backend from scratch, taking an early-stage platform to something production teams could actually rely on.

Before Ardan Labs, he was at JetBrains as a Developer Advocate for Go where he contributed to the Delve debugger and helped make GoLand the IDE that thousands of Go developers use daily.

Florin's seen firsthand how the jump from AI prototype to production system is where most projects fall apart. His workshop is built around the patterns and lessons he's picked up from shipping AI systems at companies where things have to work.

speakers.name: Garrett Denis
speakers.bio:
Garrett is a Software Engineer at Skool where he works on Go backend services that help people build and find their online community. Previously, he worked on platform teams at IDme, CrowdStrike, and AWS delivering highly-available services at scale. He’s especially interested in developer experience and using tools like CI, linting, and automation to shorten feedback loops and keep code review focused on correctness and maintainability instead of style debates.

Outside of work, Garrett is based in Southern California and is usually looking for an excuse to get outside and away from the screen, whether that’s running, hiking, backpacking, or anything in between.

speakers.name: George Adams
speakers.bio:
George Adams is a Principal Software Engineering Manager at Microsoft, where he leads the team responsible for the Microsoft build of Go and related platform integrations. His work focuses on security, cross-platform toolchain engineering, and contributing improvements back to the upstream Go project.

George previously founded AdoptOpenJDK, which became Eclipse Adoptium, now delivering over a billion OpenJDK downloads annually. Coming from a Java and open-source background, he has spent over a decade working at the intersection of large-scale enterprise engineering and community-driven development and regularly keynotes international conferences on open-source governance and secure software supply chains.

speakers.name: Ian Alexander
speakers.bio: Ian is a software engineer based in NYC, working on the Go Security team at Google.  In his spare time, he is a volunteer firefighter.

speakers.name: Jake Bailey
speakers.bio: Jake is a programming language lover and Principal Software Engineer at Microsoft. He currently works on TypeScript, mainly focusing on performance, infrastructure, and the ecosystem, along with side adventures in Go (especially compiler and runtime changes in Go and TinyGo!).

speakers.name: Jeff Lindsay
speakers.bio: Jeff Lindsay is a builder and entrepreneur most known for his work and ideas in open-source developer tooling. From webhooks to Docker, Jeff has spent much of his career building and pioneering generative primitives that let developers do more with less.

speakers.name: Johnny Boursiquot
speakers.bio: Johnny is a software engineer specializing in Go, AI engineering, cloud architecture, and distributed systems. He is a Principal Software Engineer at Stable Kernel and co-founder of a cloud-based SaaS platform focused on workforce development. He serves the Go community as a conference Program Chair for GopherCon. His work appears on platforms including O’Reilly, LinkedIn Learning, and Packt.

speakers.name: Katie Hockman
speakers.bio:
Katie has been working with Go since 2018, when she joined the Go team at Google in NYC. Katie was the tech lead for the module mirror and checksum database and worked on the security and cryptography team, where she led the design and implementation for adding native fuzzing to the language. After Google, she led the Go tracing libraries team at Datadog with heavy involvement in OpenTelemetry initiatives. 

Now Katie has moved to Tokyo, Japan, where she is working at Mercari as a software engineer on their Platform team, with a focus on making the best possible experience for Go developers.

speakers.name: Liam Hampton

talks.abstract:
Level: Intermediate

Description: AI is everywhere in our workflows now, and that raises the bar for us as Go developers. The tools are powerful - but we still have to ship code that works and keep up with a field that moves fast. How do we do both?

This workshop is the story of how I figured that out. I started as a skeptic who thought these models were just glorified autocomplete. What changed my mind was learning to treat the model like a pair programmer: an engineer who writes Go incredibly fast, but who has zero feel for the business or the context. That's where you come in - the human in the loop.

For the agent work, we won't be working on toy code. We'll use the ArdanLabs Service example as our real application - a production-style codebase that gives the agent real architecture to navigate instead of a hello-world demo.

I'll show you the things I actually do day to day:

•Context engineering - getting the right information in front of the agent, and how I work with AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md. 
•Skills - the ArdanLabs Go development skills I rely on, and how to figure out which ones are worth building for your own work. 
•Code reviews and walkthroughs - putting the agent to work understanding and critiquing code. 
•Testing - leaning on the agent for integration and black-box testing. 
•Features and refactoring - adding to existing code and giving it a proper structure. 
Structure is what makes or breaks a project in a world of agents. The Service example shows you what good structure looks like - but most real code isn't there yet. So we'll practice the fix: take a deliberately messy, unstructured project and work through restructuring it together, until the agent is noticeably better at working with it than when we started. You'll leave with a process you can take straight back to your own codebase.

For the rest, we'll work in standalone examples, small self-contained pieces of code you can lift out and reuse:

•RAG - connecting the service to a model and feeding it your own data with retrieval. 
•Tool calling and function execution - letting the model call real Go functions to hit APIs, query databases, and trigger workflows. 
•MCP - exposing those tools the standard way, with a simple MCP server in Go. 
•Optimizations - speculative decoding, semantic caching, and model routing, the things that make it fast enough to ship. 
•Security -  how to reason about the attack vectors these systems open up, from prompt injection to data exfiltration, with a hands-on look at some practical uses of LLMs in security.
What a student is expected to learn

A repeatable way to put an agent to work on a Go codebase - and the judgment to know when to trust it, when to steer it, and how to set up your projects so it can do its best work.

Prerequisites

You'll bring access to a frontier model - Anthropic, OpenAI, or any other provider with a state-of-the-art model. If you'd rather run locally, we'll use Kronk with the Qwen 3.6 35B A3B model. None of this is mandatory, but having access to a frontier model gives you the best experience - part of the skill is learning to adapt to whatever model you're given.

•Access to a frontier model, or a local setup as described below.
•Direct access to hardware which can run the workshop will be provided during the class. All the code will be OpenAI-compatible and you can run this against any environment, from Kronk to AWS Bedrock or Vertex AI and anything in-between.
•It is expected that you will have been coding in Go for several months.
•Have a functioning Go environment installed with Go 1.26 or later.
Recommended Preparation

•Before the workshop, you’ll be asked to clone a repository that will be shared with you ahead of time.
•Please read the README.md for installing all the tooling before class.
•The repository will contain some of the code that we’ll work on during the class.
•It’s recommended that you run Docker or any other container runtime as some of the dependencies will be downloaded in that format.
•To save on the bandwidth, and not rely on Internet access during the workshop, the repository will direct you on how to download and cache the models required to run the class.
•Please email the instructor,Florin Pățan, for assistance.

talks.title: Half-Day Workshop: Agents the Hard Way: Building Agentic Systems in Go (requires a separate ticket)
talks.date: August 4, 2026 at 8:00 AM PDT–12:00 PM PDT
talks.summary: Turning those calls into reliable, agentic systems is harder. Hidden state, runaway loops, hallucinated actions, and opaque frameworks introduce operational risk that doesn’t disappear…
talks.abstract:
Level: Advanced

Description: LLMs make it easy to generate code and call APIs. Turning those calls into reliable, agentic systems is harder. Hidden state, runaway loops, hallucinated actions, and opaque frameworks introduce operational risk that doesn’t disappear just because a model is involved.

This workshop takes a framework-free approach to building agentic systems in Go. We treat agents as explicit, goal-driven state machines where the LLM acts as a constrained decision component—not the system itself. Over four hours, participants will evolve a simple LLM-backed task into a controlled agent loop, implementing core building blocks by hand: state, actions, planning, execution, validation, retries, and termination conditions.

We introduce skills as capability boundaries that limit what an agent is allowed to do, and demonstrate how those skills can be backed by local Go functions or remote tools via the Model Context Protocol (MCP)—without changing the agent’s control flow. Along the way, we examine common failure modes and add guardrails to make these systems observable, testable, and safe to operate.

This workshop is designed for Go engineers who already use LLMs and want to move beyond one-off model calls toward production-ready agentic workflows they fully understand and control.

What You'll Learn

•A practical mental model for agents as goal-driven state machines
•Concrete Go patterns for implementing agent loops without frameworks
•How to design and enforce skills as explicit capability boundaries
•How to integrate MCP-backed tools while retaining control in Go
•Techniques to prevent infinite loops, hallucinated actions, and runaway costs
Prerequisites

•Familiarize yourself with Go fundamentals (Go Tour, Go by Example) 
•Introduce yourself to OpenTelemetry (optional, but recommended)
•Introduce yourself to LLMs concepts and basic Agentic concepts

talks.summary: Everything below the kernel networking stack, the container runtime, the CNI is a black box they depend on but can't observe. When something breaks in that layer, developers are stuck…
talks.abstract:
Level: Intermediate

Description: Developers own their services end-to-end in cloud-native orgs, but their visibility stops at the application boundary. Everything below the kernel networking stack, the container runtime, the CNI is a black box they depend on but can't observe. When something breaks in that layer, developers are stuck waiting on someone else.

eBPF changes that. It lets you attach programs directly to the Linux networking stack to observe traffic, measure latency, and trace failures without modifying application code, adding sidecars, or filing a ticket to the infra team.

This workshop teaches Go developers the foundational knowledge to work with eBPF and the Linux networking stack, then puts it to work. You'll build a real network observability tool in Go from scratch, using the cilium/ebpf library with bpf2go to stay in Go the entire time, no C required. Along the way, you'll develop an intuition for how packets move through the kernel, where things break, and how tools like Cilium, Hubble, and Tetragon are built under the hood.

You'll leave with a working tool and a new set of skills that combine eBPF, networking, and Go into something you can apply immediately, whether that's building developer tooling, debugging production issues, or contributing to cloud-native infrastructure projects.

Who This Workshop is For

•Go developers who build cloud-native tooling (operators, CLIs, service mesh components, CNI plugins, security tools) and want to build with eBPF, not just consume it
•SRE-developers who write Go and want to add kernel-level network visibility to their skillset
•Developers who want the foundational knowledge to understand and contribute to projects like Cilium
What You’ll Learn

•A working network observability tool written entirely in Go
•Foundational understanding of how the Linux networking stack affects your services
•Practical eBPF skills you can apply to your own tooling immediately
Prerequisites

•Comfortable writing Go
•Basic understanding of networking concepts (TCP/IP, DNS, ports, sockets)
•Familiarity with Kubernetes concepts (pods, services, namespaces)
•No prior eBPF or kernel experience required
•Optional: read the cilium/ebpf Getting Started guide (https://ebpf-go.dev/)
Recommended Preparation

•Install Docker and Kind for local Kubernetes clusters
•Have a functioning Go environment installed with Go 1.26+
•Use an editor/IDE with Go plugin installed
•Clone the workshop repository and follow the installation steps
•Please email the instructor, Donia Chaiehloudj, for assistance.

talks.abstract:
Level: All Attendees

Description: Debugging concurrent Go applications can be tricky. This is especially true in the AI Agentic coding era where more and more code is being written by the AI Agent, and the engineer plays the architect/design/review/debug roles instead. Having a solid foundation in investigative and debugging techniques, using the latest tools, becomes even more essential for the modern software engineer.

All kinds of problems can arise when concurrency and parallelism are thrown into the mix, whether it's performance bottlenecks, deadlocks, race conditions, or any other number of potential issues. Go does a lot to mitigate these issues at the language level, making concurrency easy to reason about. However, despite the convenience and ease of use afforded to us by the language, often times you may still find yourself hunting down an elusive bug involving multiple goroutines.

This workshop will dive into how to debug goroutines and channels, one of the most powerful yet complex features of Go. During the course of this workshop, you will learn how to utilize the built-in features of the Go toolchain such as the race detector and tracing tool, as well as external tools like Delve. We will learn how to use these various tools by fixing actual bugs in real time. Following each section, there will be a final Go program exhibiting a similar bug and we’ll see how the techniques we just learned can be utilized to fix the issue.

What You’ll Learn

This course is appropriate for all attendees but may be somewhat advanced for a complete beginner. Students will learn how to leverage the various tools available from the Go toolchain, standard library and beyond in order to solve their complex bugs involving multiple goroutines.

Prerequisites

A basic understanding of the Go programming language. Students do not have to be expert Go users, but they will get the most from the workshop if they are at least comfortable writing Go programs and have experience using Go’s concurrency mechanisms such as goroutines and channels.

Recommended Preparation

•Install Delve locally.
•Have a functioning Go environment installed with Go 1.24 or later.
•Have a GitHub account.
•Computers should be capable of modern software development, such as access to install and run binaries, install a code editor, etc.

Level: Intermediate

Description: Go ships with amazing profiling tools, but understanding how and when to use them, as well as understanding their output can be quite challenging.

This course was designed to take experienced Go developers and show them how to install, configure, and run the tools.  We will start with benchmarking to give us an idea of how to use the tools. Then we will work with small programs and begin to learn how to not only spot performance issues, but also how to correct them and verify the performance increases.

What You'll Learn

•Introduction and in-depth look at benchmarking, including creating benchmarks and running profiles against them.
•Install, configure, and run the pprof tools provided by Google.
•Learn about the different profiles that pprof can create, when to use them, and how to read the output of each.
•Generate profiles from live/running programs.
•Learn about torch graphs and how to read them.
•Students will cover several common performance mistakes that Go developers make learning how to spot and correct them.
Some of what you’ll work on during the workshop

•Write benchmarks for basic code samples and create profiles to determine how to increase performance.
•Generate profiles and torch graphs against live running HTTP services to determine bottlenecks and increase performance.
•Profile and debug a command line program that handles large amounts of text, and ultimately determine the bottlenecks and refactor that code to be more performant.

•Have familiarity with testing in Go

Description: 

Go has become one of the dominant languages for programming Linux systems and infrastructures. Projects like Kubernetes, containerd, Cilium, Prometheus, and the broader CNCF ecosystem use Go's ease of use to program Linux directly at the system level.

This workshop explores the functionalities available in Go to program Linux subsystems directly: from using the unsafe package to translate kernel C structs, controlling Linux devices with ioctl system calls, using zero-copy shared memory with mmap, to launching containerized processes with namespaces and cgroups - all within your Go programs.

The target audience for this workshop includes Go engineers who want to understand how Go programs interact with their Linux systems and those interested in using Go to create programs that access the kernel or control local devices.

What You'll Learn

•Using the unsafe package to convert and access C data structures
•Properly constructing ioctl to control Linux devices
•Tracing and debugging system calls
•Using mmap to map memory for zero-copy data access
•Containerized process creation and management

•Knowledge of the Go programming language
•Some familiarity with the CGo feature in Go
•Access to a Linux machine (VM or otherwise)
•Access to a GitHub account
Recommended Preparation

•While you can cross-compile, it is recommended to have access to a Linux machine with Go properly setup or WSL2 (Windows)
•An account with sudo
•Install packages linux-libc-dev, strace, drwarves

Description: One leaked database password. Four hours later, full admin access. This workshop shows you how attackers chain exploits, and how to stop them.

Using a real Go web application, you will go through the process of evaluating a real-world-like system, identifying, summarizing, and classifying the risks, vulnerabilities, and threats. Using an assumed breach scenario starting with a single stolen credential, you will then trace how one piece of vital information can pivot into broader data access and overall system compromise. Go applications in production environments have a large number of dependencies that increase their threat landscape when deployed, and as applications age, those dependencies and linkages only grow larger.

You will also learn to create and analyze data flow diagrams, identify trust boundaries, and map out attack paths – then design practical mitigations that can be implemented in their own systems. The scenario will include external services not under the control of the developer’s team or company for a real-world application of threat modeling. This ensures that the training includes black-box threat modeling as part of the exercise and deployment/development of compensating controls. Throughout this exercise, we'll use the STRIDE (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege) framework for systematic threat identification, build attack trees to visualize exploit chains, and apply risk matrices to prioritize what to fix first.

Whether you've never heard of threat modeling or done it informally for years, the goal of this workshop is to give you a framework for thinking about security in your own systems.

What You'll Learn

Threat Modeling Fundamentals

•What threat modeling is and why developers should own it
•Clear understanding of Vulnerability vs Threat vs Risk
•Using the STRIDE framework to systematically identify threats
•Creating and reading data flow diagrams (DFDs)
•Identifying trust boundaries and attack surfaces
•Mapping Identified Risks / Vulnerabilities and Weaknesses of MITRE
Attack Trees

•How attack trees complement STRIDE by mapping how threats are realized
•Visualizing attack chains from initial compromise to objective
•Identifying prerequisites and dependencies in attack paths
Credential Compromise Analysis

•Types of credentials and their “blast radius”
•Mapping lateral movement paths from a single compromised credential
•Understanding privilege escalation opportunities
•Identifying sensitive data exposure risks
Prioritization & Mitigation

•Using risk matrices to prioritize threats
•Implementing the principle of least privilege in practice
•Secrets management and rotation strategies
•Defense in depth for credential compromise
Prerequisites

•Basic understanding of three-tier web application architecture
•Familiarity with various credential types, such as API keys, tokens, passwords, and connection strings
•Comfort reading and understanding architecture diagrams
What You'll Need

•An IDE or Editor (VS Code Recommended)
•Have a functioning Go environment installed with Go 1.24+
•Docker or Docker Desktop with Docker Compose support
•A tool for diagramming (Notebooks and pens will be provided, but use what you’re most comfortable with)
•A browser with developer console access (Firefox recommended)

•Clone the example repository

talks.title: Towards Go 1.∞
talks.date: August 5, 2026 at 9:40 AM PDT–10:05 AM PDT
talks.summary: In a period of profound industry disruption, the path forward for Go is grounded in unwavering commitment to its technical foundations. Go serves as a steady hand on the tiller, not by…
talks.abstract:
In a period of profound industry disruption, the path forward for Go is grounded in unwavering commitment to its technical foundations. Go serves as a steady hand on the tiller, not by ignoring change, but by responding to it through the lens of its core principles: simplicity, reliability, efficiency, and longevity. This talk explores how we ensure Go outlasts us, thriving in this moment and into the future, remaining familiar while meeting the demands of the next decade.

The interconnected needs of human developers and coding agents are the weave and weft of the Go platform’s evolution. By combining a developer experience grounded in tools that serve developers and agents in tandem with language advancements like generic methods, json/v2, and SIMD support, we are ensuring the Go platform continues to thrive for general-purpose software engineering while also positioning Go as an ideal foundation for building high-performance AI systems.

Simultaneously, we are securing the longevity of the Go project itself by adopting a more open and scalable technical governance model that diversifies project stewardship and bridges the gap between Google and Go’s contributor community. This involves formalizing a robust contributor ladder and granting greater privileges to proven maintainers. Central to this transition is increasing the transparency of the Go proposal process through a more community-driven model, ensuring Go’s evolution remains a collaborative effort while maintaining the project’s high quality and compatibility bar.

By grounding our response to this era of disruption in Go’s core principles, we are ensuring that both the Go platform and the Go project have the foundations to thrive. Through technical excellence and open stewardship, we are building an enduring ecosystem designed to stand the test of time and remain a foundational engine for software engineering.

talks.date: August 5, 2026 at 10:05 AM PDT–10:30 AM PDT

talks.abstract:
Most Go developers learned generics when Go 1.18 shipped and haven’t thought much about them since. Fair enough. The syntax hasn’t changed much. But under the hood, recent Go releases have steadily relaxed some of the restrictions that made useful generic patterns awkward or impossible.

This talk explores the most important changes through Go 1.26, including generic type aliases, the removal of “core types” from the spec, and support for recursive type constraints. Together, these changes unlock cleaner migrations, more expressive APIs, and patterns that simply did not work in earlier versions of Go.

Along the way, we’ll look at practical examples like type-safe ordered containers, fluent builders, and generic graph traversal, with an emphasis on what these features enable in real code, not type theory.

We’ll also discuss why the Go team introduced these capabilities gradually, what tradeoffs they were protecting against, and what these changes suggest about the future direction of generics in Go.

If you learned generics when they first arrived, this session will help you catch up on what’s changed, what’s now possible, and which patterns are finally ready for production use.

talks.abstract:
What if your distributed systems knowledge could literally help save honeybee colonies? Honeybees are facing critical population declines, and inspection records are essential for hive health, swarm response, and agricultural compliance - but managing them at scale is a distributed systems problem: async IoT events, AI inference, stateful long-running processes, and real-time alerting.

In this talk, I'll walk through a working beekeeping intelligence platform I built using Go, open-source tooling, and AI. You'll see how the workflow pattern enables reliable background processing, how workflow activities cleanly wrap AI vision and audio APIs to deliver actionable hive insights, and how IoT integrations trigger real-time alerts - like detecting a captured swarm from a sudden weight delta on a hive scale.

This isn't a toy demo. It's a live system running on real hives, generating AI-powered inspection reports, classifying bee temperament from audio, and supporting an agricultural tax exemption. Through live code and a working demo, you'll leave understanding how to combine workflows and AI APIs into a coherent, reliable system - with distributed systems patterns directly transferable to your day job. The domain changes, but the architecture doesn't.

talks.title: Building Self-Optimizing Worker Pools in Go
talks.date: August 5, 2026 at 11:30 AM PDT–11:50 AM PDT
talks.summary: Whether you are a new or experience Gopher, you may know that it's easy to build a simple worker pool using Go's built in concurrency primitives. A simple naive approach will get you a…
talks.abstract:
Whether you are a new or experience Gopher, you may know that it's easy to build a simple worker pool using Go's built in concurrency primitives. A simple naive approach will get you a long way, but what if we could go deeper, and build a system that continuously optimizes itself by borrowing concepts from both mechanical engineering and biology?

In this talk, we will learn the basics of a worker pool, by building toward a real-world example of a worker pool pulling data from a remote system, then we will expose metrics that reveal import information about its performance, including the number of processed items, latency, error rate, CPU, and memory utilization.

Then we will lean into mechanical engineering concepts to build a PID (Proportional-Integral-Derivative). A PID is used for things like your car’s cruise control, or how your heat and air system responds to thermostat settings. For the purpose of this presentation, this concept will be used to control settings on the worker pool such as number of workers, batch size, and exponential backoff.

Finally, we will build a machine learning algorithm that responds to the metrics to optimize the worker pool settings during processing. For this we’ll use a set of evolutionary algorithms that respond to health signals from the worker pool’s exposed metrics.

talks.title: Inside Out: Observing Go from Code to Kernel
talks.date: August 5, 2026 at 11:50 AM PDT–12:15 PM PDT
talks.summary: Do you really know what your Go program is doing in production? From OpenTelemetry traces to pprof profiles to eBPF kernel probes, we have more observability tools than ever but when…
talks.abstract:
Do you really know what your Go program is doing in production? From OpenTelemetry traces to pprof profiles to eBPF kernel probes, we have more observability tools than ever but when should you use which one? Join Donia to see the different layers of your program, and how each comes with trade-offs in control, overhead, and depth.

In this talk, we will compare these three approaches and move from the inside of a Go application outward, from application-level traces to runtime behavior and finally to syscalls and network activity observed from the kernel. What does each layer actually reveal? What does it miss? And when should you reach for one over the others?

By the end, you will have a clear mental model of how Go programs behave across layers and a practical framework for choosing the right observability tool when debugging, optimizing, or investigating production issues.

talks.abstract:
Go plays an increasingly central role inside Microsoft, powering cloud infrastructure, developer tooling, open-source projects, and internal services used at global scale.

But running Go inside a large platform company introduces challenges most teams never encounter: multi-architecture CI, operating system integration, evolving security and compliance requirements, and the responsibility of contributing meaningfully back to the upstream project.

In this session, I’ll share how Microsoft uses Go in practice, the kinds of engineering problems we’ve had to solve, and the contributions we’ve been making to the language and toolchain. I’ll also reflect on what happens when open-source software meets enterprise-scale expectations and why strong collaboration with the Go community is essential to making it work.

This is not a product talk. It’s an honest look at Go inside Microsoft, the trade-offs, the lessons learned, and what this experience might mean for the future of Go in large organizations.

talks.abstract:
The Life, Death, and Rebirth of testing/quick | Akshay Shah, Antithesis

Abstract: When the Go authors designed the standard library, they didn’t just include net/http, encoding/json, and basic testing - they also included testing/quick, a little-known package for property-based testing. In this talk, we’ll explore what property-based testing is, how to use testing/quick, and why the standard library package was eventually frozen.

Talk/Attendee Level: Intermediate




Three Simple Data Structures Built on Slices | Simon Law, Tailscale

Abstract: The humble slice is a familiar friend to any Go programmer. But did you know that you can build stacks, circular queues, and priority queues on top of a slice from memory? Amaze your friends and impress your colleagues as you do a little typing instead of importing a little dependency.

Talk/Attendee Level: All Attendees




Unix Pipes are Better Than Agents | Derick Schaefer

Abstract: The industry is racing to give LLMs more tools, APIs, and agent frameworks. Reserve, a Go CLI for exploring FRED macroeconomic data, takes the opposite approach: enabling the tool to explain itself. Every command can expose context, intent, examples, and pipeline patterns, allowing models to discover functionality, compose deterministic workflows, and explain exactly how a result was produced. Rather than letting an agent reason over commands, flags, and raw APIs, Reserve pushes collection, transformation, and analysis into deterministic, reproducible Unix pipelines, preserving precious tokens for insight rather than orchestration. The outcome is simpler, more transparent, and surprisingly powerful. The industry keeps asking how much intelligence can be embedded in upstream orchestration, while the Unix philosophy has spent the last fifty years moving orchestration into composition.

Talk/Attendee Level:  All Attendees




h.Sum(data) Does Not Hash Data | Ruslan Kadyrov, Mercari, Inc.

Abstract: In this lightning talk, I’ll walk through how I misunderstood Go’s hash.Hash interface, why the mistake looked perfectly reasonable, and what it reveals about Go’s API design. We’ll explore common hashing footguns, the difference between sha256.Sum256 and streaming hashers, and why small misunderstandings in low-level APIs can quietly produce incorrect behavior in production systems.

Talk/Attendee Level: All Attendees




Hunting Dead Code in Production | Navneet Anand, Uber

Abstract: If your service is instrumented, you can ask it - at any moment, in any environment - what lines have actually executed. This talk shows how to build a coverage-driven dead-code detector for any Go service in roughly 100 lines of standard-library Go: an HTTP handler that snapshots counters on demand, a reset endpoint for time-windowed analysis, and a small unifier that merges profiles across multiple builds. I’ll close with the failure modes that turn a coverage signal into a confidence score, not a verdict.

Talk/Attendee Level: Intermediate




The Journey of Connecting Japan to the Global Go Community | Takuto Nagami, Chiba Institute of Technology

Abstract: Many Japanese Gophers dream of engaging with the global Go community, but language barriers often hold them back from taking the leap.

Through the Gophers EX project, I've spent the past year helping Japanese Gophers overcome those barriers and participate in international conferences as attendees or speakers. Along the way, we realized that true connection works both ways: it isn't just about sending people abroad, it's also about bringing the world to Japan.

In this lightning talk, I'll share that journey, what we learned from it, and how it eventually led to the launch of GopherCon Japan.

Abstract:The sizespecializedmalloc GOEXPERIMENT will be enabled by default in Go 1.27. We’ll go over what it is and how we added it and how it should make memory allocation in your Go programs faster.

talks.abstract:
Testing concurrent code has always been a balance between tests being either hacky, flaky or slow. While the testing/synctest package made it possible for us to more effectively write idiomatic, easy-to-read tests for our concurrent programs that are both reliable and fast, it also came with a set of constraints.

In this talk, we’ll look at exactly what synctest can and cannot do, the underlying reasons behind its limitations, and how to avoid them. Finally, using a real-world example, we’ll see how proper use can push us towards robust system design we can feel confident about. In short, you’ll know precisely what to do to make the most of synctest, and why that will make your application code better.

talks.title: Reimagining Plan 9 from Bell Labs for WebAssembly
talks.date: August 5, 2026 at 2:50 PM PDT–3:15 PM PDT
talks.summary: Plan 9 from Bell Labs is the most influential operating system you've never used. Developed as the successor to Unix by the same team, Plan 9 explored how far a small set of carefully…
talks.abstract:
Plan 9 from Bell Labs is the most influential operating system you've never used. Developed as the successor to Unix by the same team, Plan 9 explored how far a small set of carefully chosen abstractions could go: all system capabilities represented via the filesystem, customized per-process, and assembled from resources scattered across the network.

What if we took those core ideas and re-applied them to the web using Go and WebAssembly?

This talk will deconstruct and re-synthesize the design principles behind Plan 9. Rather than porting an operating system, we'll look at how its abstractions can be reimagined with Go as a modern software primitive that makes Plan 9's ideas usable and explorable in the browser and beyond.

Through stories and demos, attendees will learn:
- What made Plan 9's abstractions so radical, and why they still matter
- Why Go and WebAssembly are uniquely good for revisiting these ideas
- How we can finally bridge the world of Unix and the web

No prior experience with Plan 9 or WebAssembly is required, just an interest in building systems that are thoughtfully designed and built to last.

talks.abstract:
The trickiest and hardest-to-identify bugs are often those fixable with a single line of code. Hours, days, or months can be spent only to find a missing Unlock() in the (dead) end. After I suffered such a case, I asked myself two questions: "Am I using mutexes wrong?" and "How can I prevent bugs like this in the future?"

The search for answers led me to the depths of static analysis and an exploration of Go mutex usage patterns in the wild.

In my talk, I want to share my findings and present a new linter for detecting mutex misuse.

talks.date: August 5, 2026 at 4:15 PM PDT–4:40 PM PDT
talks.summary: Tree-sitter powers syntax highlighting, navigation, and code intelligence across modern editors. But in Go, using it usually means bringing C along for the ride. That is fine until you…
talks.abstract:
Tree-sitter powers syntax highlighting, navigation, and code intelligence across modern editors. But in Go, using it usually means bringing C along for the ride. That is fine until you cross-compile, target WASM, or try to ship one clean static binary.

This talk is the story of building a pure-Go Tree-sitter runtime, and of learning how to trust it. Much of the implementation was AI-assisted, but the interesting part is not that an LLM wrote code. The interesting part is the harness around it: parity checks against the C runtime, benchmarks that catch fake wins, reproduction tests for every bug, and regression gates that force correctness to keep moving forward.

The runtime now supports hundreds of embedded grammars, hand-written external scanners, incremental parsing, queries, and a self-hosting grammar compiler. Full parses trade some raw speed for portability, while common editor-style incremental workloads can be dramatically faster than the C path.

Come for the parser internals; stay for the practical lessons on using LLMs in serious systems code without handwaving. This is a case study in moving quickly while keeping evidence close enough to know when the code is actually getting better.

talks.abstract:
Last year, we shared the story of TypeScript's port to Go. A lot has happened since then: we've shipped TypeScript 6.0 as a bridge release, watched our native preview grow past 5 million weekly downloads. The port is done, but the work didn't stop there.

In this talk, we'll go beyond the port itself. We'll cover the new API surfaces we've built on top of the Go codebase, including a snapshot-based language server, cross-language IPC, and Wasm. We'll talk about how the community has adopted the new compiler, how we've ensured stability at scale, and what surprises and compromises came up along the way. We'll also share our continued experience writing Go; where the language and toolchain have gotten better for us, and where they sometimes haven't.

talks.abstract:
The world of cryptography is undergoing changes faster than it ever did in most of our careers, but the Go cryptography maintainers are working to keep your applications secure with the least possible amount of disruption.

We’ll talk about our new ML-DSA package and how we test it, about how we are preparing for the post-quantum transition, about the new HPKE package, about randomness and entropy, about secure erasure of ephemeral secrets with runtime/secret, and about a nuanced and complex security issue in crypto/tls we’ve had to deal with.

This is your yearly appointment to learn about the progress of Go’s cryptography libraries, and the techniques we use to maintain them.

talks.abstract:
In 2023, Go 1.21 officially introduced the log/slog package, real structured logging in the standard library that many of us had been waiting years for. It covers the fundamentals well, but there are gaps that can become painful in real-world, large-scale systems. This talk explores two extensions, built on the slog.Handler interface, that fill some of those gaps. Some Gophers might even argue they should be part of the log/slog package itself.

First, a custom slog.Handler implementation that integrates slog with testing.T, routing the logs to the test's output. This has the nice effect of suppressing log noise during passing tests while surfacing full "production" logs on failure. We will cover the handler code itself, then dive into several tricky edge cases and how they were addressed.

Second, a dynamic per-component log leveling system that lets you change the log verbosity for individual components or subsystems at runtime, with no restarts and no performance penalty. If you've ever enabled DEBUG logging for your service to troubleshoot an issue and been buried in an avalanche of logs completely obscuring the ones you care about, you won't want to miss this.

talks.title: Sandboxing DuckDB with io/fs
talks.date: August 6, 2026 at 11:45 AM PDT–12:10 PM PDT
talks.summary: Go programs that embed C libraries face a hidden trap: the C library brings its own I/O stack. It doesn't know about your credentials, your TLS configuration, your request tracing, or…
talks.abstract:
Go programs that embed C libraries face a hidden trap: the C library brings its own I/O stack. It doesn't know about your credentials, your TLS configuration, your request tracing, or your retry logic. It just reaches out to the network or disk on its own terms. You end up with two parallel I/O systems in the same binary, and they will drift apart in ways that are hard to debug and expensive to maintain.

DuckDB is a great example. It is one of the most useful embedded databases available today, and many Go programs are starting to use it. But DuckDB ships extensions like httpfs and aws that perform network I/O directly from C++. If your Go program wraps those extensions, you have lost observability, lost credential management, and lost the ability to apply standard Go middleware to the database's I/O operations.

The solution is simpler than it looks. Go's io/fs interface, introduced in 1.16, gives us a clean, composable abstraction for read-only file systems. Most C libraries that do I/O support some form of virtual file system hook. If you can connect those two things, you can route all of the library's I/O back through the Go runtime, and suddenly every cloud SDK, every telemetry wrapper, every retry policy you have already written becomes available to the database too.

This talk teaches you how to do that. We will walk through the split stack problem in concrete terms, look at how DuckDB's virtual file system API works, and build a mental model of the bridge: a small C++ extension that intercepts DuckDB's file operations and forwards them to a Go function that satisfies io/fs. By the end, you will understand the pattern well enough to apply it to other C libraries, and you will learn about an open-source library that does it for DuckDB today.

talks.abstract:
Every import statement is a transaction, but most of us never check the receipt. 

In this talk, we'll follow your dependencies from go.mod all the way to compiled symbols, uncovering what the Go linker actually pulls into your binary, where Dead Code Elimination saves you, and where it fails. Along the way, we'll expose the patterns secretly inflating your binary size and explain why that bloat even matters. 

Whether you're a library maintainer, a product engineer, or both, you'll walk away with a toolkit for evaluating dependencies so your binaries stay lean.

talks.abstract:
Perform Inference Directly in Your Go Applications with Kronk | Bill Kennedy, Ardan Labs

Abstract: Self-hosted inference — running models on hardware you control — means no per-token costs, no data leaving your environment, no vendor lock-in, and access to the long tail of open-source models that go well beyond the LLMs everyone is talking about. And contrary to popular belief, you don't need a GPU rack: small models like Qwen3.5-0.8B-Q8_0 run comfortably on the same laptop you're using right now. The hard part has been doing it from Go without CGO, Python, or a network hop to something like Ollama.

 In this lighting talk I will show you how you can use Kronk to perform inference directly in your go applications.

Talk/Attendee Level: All Attendees




A Small Update About TinyGo | Ron Evans, The Hybrid Group

Abstract: The latest and greatest about TinyGo, the Go compiler for the smallest of places.

Talk/Attendee Level: All Attendees




Creating a full desktop environment with Go! | Andrew Williams, Apptrix.ai

Abstract: What if you could be using Go to build apps on your laptop - what if the entire desktop was written with Go? This presentation highlights the benefits and beauty of a desktop environment created purely with Go. This whistle-stop tour of a massive topic covers lots of tantalising details, providing some code snippets and lots of screenshots to illustrate the topic. We leave with a "try it out and contribute" call to action and a great reveal. 🙂

Talk/Attendee Level: All Attendees




Nip the Nits in the Bud | Garrett Denis, Skool

Abstract: Repeated "nit" comments - line wrapping, formatting, style preferences - are easy to follow but tedious to enforce by hand, and every one of them steals reviewer attention from correctness, design, and risk. In this lightning talk I'll turn one real nit from our codebase - enforcing one clause per line in boolean conditionals - into a custom Go linter using `go/analysis`, complete with an auto-fix and golangci-lint integration, in a single worked example. The point isn't the rule, it's that the  pattern is repeatable. If a style choice is objective and recurring, it belongs in tooling, not a review thread. As AI assistants generate ever more code, codifying your team's conventions as lint rules is how you keep both humans and machines consistent - and keep review focused on what actually matters.

Talk/Attendee Level: All Attendees




AI is a Power-up, Not a Player | Seth Lumnah, Capital One

Abstract: I maintain shared Go libraries used across a large organization, and the bottleneck has never been code—it's attention. Proposals pile up, PRs wait for review, and community updates never get written because compiling them takes too long. So I started writing agent skills: markdown files that point an AI at our style guide and tell it how to handle routine work. This talk tours the skills I actually use, the discipline that keeps reviews honest, and the foundation work that any maintainer can start tomorrow. AI is a power-up, not a player.

Talk/Attendee Level:  All Attendees




Safer Agent Infrastructure: Don't Give the Agent Your Keys! | Marc Dougherty, Go Team, Google

Abstract: AI agents today are desktop software, acting directly with a user's credentials. This has led to auth token leaks and unexpected behaviors that reach the news. How can you avoid making the headlines? Better authentication, and management of delegated credentials is the first step. Learn some tactics for keeping the keys away from your agents, and other ways to make your agent infrastructure more mature (and a bit safer!).

Go's tooling ecosystem is evolving beyond simply finding problems to automatically fixing them, but security analysis has lagged behind. In this session, we'll explore a new AI-ready taint analysis engine for gosec that traces untrusted data across an entire Go application, accurately detecting vulnerabilities such as SQL injection, command injection, path traversal, SSRF, XSS, and more.

Attendees will learn how SSA- and call graph-based analysis makes data flow tracking practical in Go, how these techniques dramatically reduce false positives, and how the same architecture can power automated and AI-assisted remediation. See where Go security tooling is headed: from detecting vulnerabilities to tracing, understanding, and fixing them before they reach production.

talks.title: Chasing the Moon: Engineering a High-Performance Lua VM in Pure Go
talks.date: August 6, 2026 at 4:05 PM PDT–4:30 PM PDT
talks.summary: Lua is widely used for embedded scripting, providing extensibility in systems such as Neovim, Redis, and Nginx. However, embedding C-based Lua implementations such as PUC Lua in Go…
talks.abstract:
Lua is widely used for embedded scripting, providing extensibility in systems such as Neovim, Redis, and Nginx. However, embedding C-based Lua implementations such as PUC Lua in Go introduces CGO build complexity and call overhead. Existing pure-Go implementations are easier to embed, but are typically 2–3 fold slower than PUC Lua and consume significantly more memory. 

This talk introduces a new pure-Go, register-based Lua VM that achieves performance within 30–50% of PUC Lua while remaining fully CGO-free. Rather than focusing solely on VM internals, the session uses the VM as a case study in high-performance Go systems programming, covering techniques applicable far beyond interpreter design including memory layout optimization, GCpressure reduction, elimination of hidden allocations, and construction of cache-friendly data structures. 

The talk will also demonstrate practical optimization workflows using Go benchmarks, CPU and memory profiling, escape analysis, and compiler inlining diagnostics.

talks.title: Building a Durable Agent & MCP Execution Engine in Go
talks.date: August 6, 2026 at 4:35 PM PDT–5:00 PM PDT

talks.abstract:
AI agents can call tools, invoke APIs, and connect to remote systems through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). But most agentic frameworks aren't durable - if the process crashes mid tool call, execution is lost, context is gone, and the agent starts over from scratch. That’s costly. MCP makes this worse: a tool call isn't always a single round-trip. Servers can pause execution mid-call to request user input (aka elicitation) or trigger an LLM completion (aka sampling). Both of these are interactions that can suspend for minutes before resuming. A simple retry loop can't model these human interactions required, or the durability to resume the agent loop.

In this talk, we'll explore the fundamental building blocks backing our fully durable agent and MCP execution engine written in Go. We'll cover deterministic replay, checkpoint-based resumption, how the Virtual Actor pattern and Go’s primitives power the underlying durability engine, and how we embedded a transparent and built-in MCP durability worker.

You'll leave with a concrete understanding of what durable execution actually means and looks like in Go for Agents and MCP, and why it's the right foundation you need to run in production in the AI era that we find ourselves in today.
